runs.text: Travis Kim
Old Delivery
I traced my finger down the hood of my car which was fuzzy with pollen and I felt its waste and the sickly smell of the dried red
treefruits

stamped into the ridges of the concrete. I went back inside to get some frozen water bottles and a cassette tape. I taped the bottles under the air conditioning which was only on to cool the locked crate in the back seat. As the car sputtered to life its vents coughed a wave of mildew into my face and I opened the windows in disgust. The sun-heated tarmac burned my tires as the car peeled off the driveway, and the cassette player began playing a rock song I hadn’t heard since I last saw Richie.

Driving out of Hayward was a battle of potholes, merges, and a dried stick of gum which broke brittle in my mouth and lost its flavor in two minutes. By the time I’d crossed the bridge, the tape was on its third loop because I’d only recorded two songs onto it and I felt like the guitar pick was scraping the hairs out of the inside of my ear. Richie hated this kind of music. He always turned it off whenever I listened to it at home. I sat for a second and turned the music off too.
The sun lay directly overhead. I paced a tan stained Chevy Suburban which reminded me of the same one he drove back when I worked for him. We
did

photos. Family pictures and the like. Fussy child clawing his collars that his mom fixed up for him standing next to the dad and uncle who had called three weeks in advance to schedule a time because the grandparents were flying in from Pennsylvania and after they landed they brought Hershey’s kisses and a little sticker of the Liberty Bell with its exaggerated crack down the middle and now they looked over the grandson, their skin their bones ragdolled on the floor shirt untucked crying about some picture that wouldn’t mean anything to him until he was thirty-one, how fortunate. I didn’t know what to do in these situations so Richie would come in and offer the kids more Hershey’s kisses and give me a look on the way out that said more in anger than words would. All I would do then was set the focus and fire some pictures off. The kids would wince at the flash.

I was tired of thinking about Richie so I turned the music back on. One of the water bottles started leaking. Cool water spilled down my leg and I shivered. I looked back at the crate, worried that it would overheat, before turning back to stare at the mess of concrete slabs lining the interchange, one of which led to the airport. We’d only been on an airplane once which was before I could remember. When he came here he told them he was my father and they believed it because he was really good at pretending. He could snap out of it and pretend that nothing was wrong so they never knew. But the instant it was just me and him it all melted away and he began to say things. He would look at me and realize I wasn’t his son and demanded I call him uncle instead, well of course, he wasn’t married, he’d never had kids, and he’d hit me or throw me out of the house, lock me out in the rain and make me sleep outside before waking up and realizing what he’d done. I’d huddle up on the porch and bundle myself up on the wicker-backed chair with no cushion and wake up to him shaking me and asking what was wrong. At times he’d forget about me, going home without me and leaving me at work or dropping me off at school and not coming back. And at others he’d want to know where I was at all times, growing frantic when I wasn’t in front of him. He’d wake up screaming and run to my room to grab me, making me run out of the house where he’d stand in the middle of the street and pant his exhaustion. It got worse as he got older. It got so bad one day I just left.

I checked my map and realized I had taken the wrong exit. I looked back at the locked crate in my back seat and it looked back at me with its dark blue ridges. I took a U-turn and began to drive back to the highway. Richie would always go on these damn walks and tell me that he always walked on both directions of sidewalks because the different perspectives made the scene look different. That was a lie. The road looked exactly the same. Wiper fluid spilled out onto my windshield and the wipers made a scratching sound as leftover pollen congealed into a mush which fought to remain on the glass. It took me three repetitions to clear the windshield yet the road still looked the exact, yellow, same. The flower beds on the side of the road were still dried up and overrun with weeds and vines.

I took the right exit this time and as I kept driving trees began to show themselves then turned to forests atop winding hills with more blind turns than the reflectors on the double yellow lines. A burgundy sedan took a turn too sharply and I slammed on the brakes. It whizzed past me and I caught a glimpse of the driver who was crying. I checked my navigation. Eighteen minutes to the destination. The sun was low in the sky and its rays peered through the gaps in the trees, spilling golden light onto the ground and into the car. I looked back at the crate. It was still there. I slammed the breaks again and a squirrel skittered across the road.

I wasn’t going to go, I’d told him I wouldn’t see him again, but he sent me a letter. I knew it was him from the handwriting: "Come see me nephew, I want to see you again before I die." That was it, no apology, no explanation, just those thirteen words. I ignored it at first, but one time I was doing another one of these deliveries and I got pulled over. As I was digging through my glove department to find my registration, an old photo fell out. It was from when I graduated high school and Richie was standing next to me with the biggest smile on his face. I thought about that same smile when he gave those kids the Hershey's kisses and I thought about their family and how their grandparents had flown in just for a picture and how if Richie died then there'd be nobody for me to take pictures with, not that that bothered me much since I was already living alone but I figured since he was my uncle, but actually my father since I was six, my boss since I was twelve, my friend at times and the person I hated most at others, I at least owed him a visit before I wouldn't get a chance to see him again. So when I saw his name on the ledger I ran to my supervisor's office and told him that although I wasn't his best employee I did a pretty good job and never asked for much so I was wondering if it would be okay if I take this one job for myself even though it was out of the way.

The second to last time I saw Richie was three years ago. At the time I’d started gardening because a client that I’d brought in gave me a planter with a tiny potato plant as a gift and told me that it’d be worthwhile to give gardening a shot. I figured it wouldn’t be too much trouble, so I went to the library and got this little book on gardening. I didn’t know at the time that there were so many things you had to do to grow a little potato. Things like slightly acidic and well-drained soil, the right levels of sunlight, constant moisture, fertilizer without too much nitrogen. All sorts of little things just to keep the plant alive. But it was distracting and let me keep my mind off of Richie, especially as his condition worsened. It became a big love of mine, to take care of the plant.

The day the leaves of the potato plant withered away I came home to see the floor covered with dirt and Richie squatting in the middle of the living room with the remains of my plant in his hands. He sat there barefoot but in his work clothes scrabbling at the dirt as if it wasn’t already stretched thin on the ground, flecks of linoleum seeping between the loam and white dirt pebbles. The plant itself lay in diced chunks with flaky leaves scattered to the kitchen table and a pair of scissors sat nearby. I called out his name, faintly at first then a yell but he didn’t look up at me. I sat down at the kitchen table and watched him continue to paw at the ground, creating mounds of clay which he’d sift his fingers through as if in search of some lost treasure. Bile rose to my throat and I walked through the house while he ignored me and I packed my bags. For good measure I took the graduation picture out of its frame and kept that too because it seemed like he’d already forgotten me. That day I grabbed my car keys and didn’t look back when I drove away.

The sun was setting and I almost missed the driveway to his house. I swerved and sideswiped the mailbox which was already leaning too far to the side. I drove up the steep driveway and scraped the underbelly of my car when the asphalt transitioned to gravel. I put the car in park and grabbed the crate.

I rang the doorbell three times before the hospice nurse came and told me it was too late. I stood there with a crate full of morphine in my hand while the nurse reassured me that it was not my fault and that “the patient” had passed just a few minutes ago.

After explaining my relation to Richie they let me in to see him. He looked thinner. His skin fell like foil across his bones and his mouth stuck agape as if air still moved between the lips which faded into a gray pallor. Tubular lines stuck out of his nose and down his shirt and though he hadn’t been that old I saw his wrinkles for the first time. I saw the way his eyelids sat drooping and swollen with age and the gaunt hollow of his cheeks where the skin seemed to sink into his skull. Atop his head were the few remaining strands of hair, grayed out and wiry, and centered on his face sat his crooked nose which he’d broken slamming his face onto a table. He lay in an incline atop pillows which seemed too large for his head and his hospital gown draped over his body like a bedsheet before dissolving into the blankets which crumpled at his waist and down the bed.

I stood there with the crate still in my hands. I looked at him as if I’d never met him before. Who was this man who’d nearly died grabbing his nephew out of the debris and finding his way to America, never letting go of his nephew’s hand whose father was the older brother he hated for convincing him to leave home to fight in war and come back to their parents dead, and he, the younger brother, the last standing, with no photos of the family, the family that faded from his memory torn apart by war and time, photographing families his whole life with the hope that he’d be able to remember his own but only forgetting more and more until he’d torn apart his nephew’s potato plants because he thought his family was buried there, between the particles of dirt mashed and stretched on the ground he’d cried on, realizing that even if he found a picture of his family it wouldn’t mean anything to him because he couldn’t recognize them any longer, that he couldn’t even picture his mother’s face anymore, and realizing days after that his nephew was gone too and so too was his nephew fading from his memory and though he knew that he hadn’t been the right person to live with or the right boss or the right uncle or the right father he wanted to see his nephew again because he was the last face that he could fight the forgetting with so he sent the letter but it was too late. So I stood there and looked at him for the first time.

I looked next to his bed and I saw on the bedframe an old EtchASketch and an empty picture frame, the same picture frame I’d taken the graduation picture out of. In all the years of our life together as a photographer and his assistant, that was all we had. Not once had we thought it a good idea to take a picture of ourselves in the decade we shared together in that studio. I wondered if he remembered what I looked like before he died.

I mumbled my blind thanks to the nurses as I left the house and walked outside. At this point the sun was setting and tinged the tree branches orange. I put the crate down on the gravel and sat on it, watching the sun bury itself behind a mountain. I coughed and spit my gum out onto the ground before covering it with a rock. As if in response, a nighthawk yelped in the distance to no answer and continued its screeching until I got up and left. As I drove off I glanced in my rearview mirror and saw the mailbox lying on its side with papers spilling out of it.

The drive to the hospital was largely uneventful. I drove back in silence broken by the occasional angry honk and bump on the road. Streetlamps lit up the San Mateo Bridge while brakelights and headbeams flickered back and forth. Talk about a road which looked the same from here to there and back whichever which way here was and there was. It was a crumbling concrete aberration lodged into the shelves of the nightdark bay, curving in whatever directions they decided it was best to jam concrete-rebar columns down in order to carry thirteen miles and thousands of tons of metal and plastic and oil and flesh. I looked back one last time at the crate behind me, hoping it would disappear.

I got to the hospital and returned the crate before logging my hours and mileage on a clipboard. The sterilizing hospital lights burned my eyes and it hurt to close them and even more to open them. I hung the clipboard back on the wall and trudged back to my car. As I started the car the air conditioning turned on again and the same mildewy scent from the bowels of my decaying car smashed into my nostrils and I coughed. Salty phlegm rose to my mouth and I spit it out the window.

Richie opened the photography shop in December of 1961. A year later, during Christmas of 1962, he counted his sales and got me my first and only Christmas present. It was an EtchASketch, a toy which I spent hours on, creating all sorts of drawings, starting with lines and boxes before progressing to little houses, faces, and eventually, the last thing I drew: a family. I don’t remember what exactly compelled me to draw them the way I did. I’m pretty sure I was just reading a magazine and tried to copy one of its illustrations. It was a peculiar family because there were, just like the Pennsylvania grandparents family, two grandparents, two brothers, one of them married, and one grandson, the last child. After I drew that family I remember losing my EtchASketch. No matter where I looked I couldn’t find it. To make me feel better, Richie told me that my drawing was so good that the family had gotten up and out of the EtchASketch and walked away.

But on his bedstand, next to the empty picture frame was that same EtchASketch. Somehow he’d kept it from erasing itself for nearly two decades. As I drove I held it tightly in my right hand, in constant fear that the motion of the car would mess up the drawing. For I held in my hand my family, all that was left of them in this world, all I had and all I was. As I drove past familiar street signs I realized that for the first time, I was alone in the world.
